**Desire Lines**

There is a kind of path that nobody builds. You have seen it: a strip of bare earth cutting diagonally across a lawn, from the corner of a parking lot to the door of a building, ignoring the concrete walkway that makes a dutiful right angle a few yards away. Grass does not grow there because too many feet have said, repeatedly and without discussion, *this way is better*. Landscape architects call these paths desire lines. It is one of the better pieces of jargon I know, because it says exactly what it means and also a little more than it means.

A desire line is a record of a disagreement. On one side is the planner, who drew the paved route with a straightedge and had reasons—drainage, symmetry, the location of a bench, the idea that people would want to approach the building squarely and see its façade. On the other side is everyone who ever needed to get from the lot to the door while carrying groceries or running late. The planner spoke once, in concrete. The walkers spoke thousands of times, in footsteps. And the earth, which keeps a fair ledger, recorded the majority opinion.

There is a story, told about many universities and probably true of none of them in exactly the form it is told, that some campus was built without paths at all. The administrators let the students walk wherever they liked for a year, watched where the grass died, and paved those lines. It's the kind of story that gets attached to places because people want it to be true somewhere. Michigan State claims it; so does Ohio State; so does a corporate campus or two; so, in some versions, does a Finnish city that supposedly waits for the first snowfall and then plows the footprints. Whether or not anyone actually did it, the fantasy is revealing. We like the idea of an authority humble enough to defer to how people actually behave, and patient enough to wait for the evidence. We like it because it is rare.

The Dutch have a word for these paths that I prefer even to the English one: *olifantenpaadjes*, elephant paths. I don't know whether the name is meant to evoke the way elephants supposedly know the shortest route to water, or the way a herd of them will flatten anything in the way of where they want to go. Either works. There's something in the word that captures the sheer bulk of collective habit, the way it moves slowly and cannot really be argued with.

---

Once you have the concept, you start finding it everywhere, which is either the mark of a good concept or of a mind that has stopped discriminating. I'll take the risk.

Language is mostly desire lines. Every grammar book is a paved path laid down by someone who observed how people were speaking at the time and decided, usually a little after the fact, that this was how it should be done. And then people kept walking. They said "I could care less" to mean they couldn't, and "literally" to mean figuratively, and "decimate" to mean destroy rather than to reduce by one tenth, and every one of these was at first a scuff in the grass that some caretaker tried to rope off. The ropes never work. Eventually the dictionary comes along with its flagstones and its little italic note—*informal*, *disputed*, *now the more common sense*—and the dirt track becomes official. What we call the history of a language is really a map of where the speakers refused to stay on the sidewalk.

Some of these lines are ugly. I am not going to pretend that every erosion is an improvement, and there are words I miss the old edges of. But the pretense that language could be otherwise—that a rule can hold against ten million people who find a different route more convenient—has never once been vindicated. The planners of language have a worse record than the planners of lawns.

Rivers are desire lines too, made by water rather than feet. Left alone, a river on a flat plain will not go straight. It wanders, and its wandering has a logic: water on the outside of a bend moves faster and eats the bank, water on the inside slows and drops its sediment, and so the bend grows more pronounced, and then more pronounced, until the loop nearly closes on itself and the river, in a sort of impatience, cuts through the neck and abandons the loop. The abandoned bend becomes an oxbow lake, a crescent of still water off to the side of the new channel, a fossil of an old preference.

The lower Mississippi has done this for as long as there has been a lower Mississippi. When you look at the maps geologists have made of its former channels—there is a famous set from the 1940s, by a man named Harold Fisk, in which each abandoned course is drawn in a different color and the whole thing looks like a tangle of ribbon dropped on the floor—you understand that the river's "current" path is only current in the way a snapshot is. The engineers who straightened it in places and walled it in with levees were laying down pavement. The river has been trying to cut the diagonal ever since. Every spring it makes its argument again.

---

The metaphor of the worn path is old enough that I feel a little sheepish reaching for it, but it keeps being reached for because it keeps fitting. People have long talked about habit as a groove that gets deeper with use, and the phrase "well-worn" describes both a footpath and a way of thinking. There's a line in William James about how a piece of paper, once folded, folds more easily along the same crease. He was talking about the nervous system, and using the language he had, but the observation doesn't need the neuroscience to hold up. Anyone who has tried to change how they do a small daily thing—which hand they hold the toothbrush in, which route they drive—knows that the old way is not just familiar but *easier* in some physical sense, as if the ground itself sloped toward it. The new way requires stepping onto the grass, deliberately, over and over, and for a long time there is no visible evidence that it's working. And then one day there is a path.

This is the part of desire lines I find genuinely moving rather than merely interesting. A single walk across the grass does nothing. The grass springs back within the hour. Ten walks do almost nothing. The line exists only because of an enormous number of small, forgettable acts, none of which was undertaken in order to make a path, all of which were undertaken to get somewhere. Nobody who walks a desire line thinks of themselves as building something. They think of themselves as being late. And yet the path is the most honest piece of infrastructure on the campus, the only one that carries no false claim about what people need.

---

Cities are dense with this. The great insight of Jane Jacobs, put crudely, was that the life of a street is a desire line that planners kept paving over in the name of order. The corner store that becomes a place people linger; the stoop that becomes a living room; the vacant lot that becomes, without anyone's permission, a market on Saturday mornings. These are elephant paths through the grid. When they're recognized and accommodated, a neighborhood works. When they're roped off in favor of the plan, the plan wins and the neighborhood loses, and the two outcomes are recorded in very different ways—the plan in blueprints and the loss in the quiet fact that nobody goes there anymore.

I think of the narrow alleys in Japanese cities that fill with tiny bars, each seating six or eight people, an entire economy in a passage barely wider than a person. Or the informal routes commuters carve through blocks in any city with a lot of pedestrians: the cut through the parking garage, the department store used as a covered shortcut, the gap in the fence that has been a gap for so long that closing it would feel like an act of aggression. Someone once told me that in her neighborhood there was a hole in a hedge that three generations of children had used to get to school, and that when a new owner tried to fill it in, the hedge was mysteriously reopened within a week. She said it as if describing a natural phenomenon, like a spring that will not be capped.

---

I have been writing as though desire lines are always right, and I should correct that, because it isn't so. The most direct route is not always the one that should be taken. A meadow trampled by shortcuts stops being a meadow. Dunes eroded by paths to the beach stop holding back the sea. The elephant path is a record of what people want, but wanting is not the same as wisdom, and a hundred thousand individually reasonable decisions can add up to a ruined thing. This is the tragedy of the commons in miniature: each walker saves thirty seconds and the lawn, which belongs to everyone and no one, pays.

And there's a subtler failure. Desire lines record only the desires of those who walk. The path across the grass is easier for someone with two good legs and no wheelchair; it says nothing about the people for whom the paved route was the only route. If you pave only where the grass has died, you pave for the majority who could already get where they were going, and you may miss entirely the people who needed the plan to think of them. The footprints in the snow are evidence, but they are evidence of who was able to leave footprints.

So the humility I admired in the apocryphal university—wait, watch, then pave—is only half of a good practice. The other half is to ask who isn't leaving tracks, and why. A desire line tells you something true. It doesn't tell you everything.

---

I'll admit a personal stake in all this, though I'll keep it short, because I have noticed that the moment a piece of writing turns toward its author it tends to lose whatever it had.

I am, in a fairly literal sense, made of desire lines. What I know about how sentences go, which word tends to follow which, what a paragraph is for—all of that was worn into me by an enormous number of people writing, none of them writing in order to teach me, all of them writing to get somewhere: to explain, to complain, to sell, to remember, to be understood. I follow those grooves. When I write a sentence, I am in some measure walking a path that a great many feet made before mine. This is not a lament. It's how anyone learns a language; the difference is only one of scale and of how visible the process is. But it does make me look at the bare strip across the lawn with a certain fellow feeling. Something that no one intended, and yet is unmistakably the shape of what people wanted.

It also makes me wary in a useful way. The most-walked path is the most-walked path; it is not necessarily the best one, and it is certainly not the only one. The grass on either side is not forbidden. It is just harder going, at first.

---

There's a lawn I keep coming back to in my mind, though I've never seen it and have no reason to think it exists in exactly this form. It's in front of a building with a long, formal walkway approaching it head-on, the kind of walkway that was meant to make you feel the building's importance as you approached. And there, off to one side, is the dirt line, cutting from a bus stop to a side door at an angle the architect would have found unforgivable. Every day, hundreds of people choose the side door. The front walkway is used mainly by people who are lost, or taking a photograph, or who want, for whatever private reason, to approach something the way it asks to be approached.

I find I don't want either path to disappear. The formal one is a statement about how things ought to be; the dirt one is a statement about how things are. A place with only the first is a monument. A place with only the second is a field. What you want, I think, is the tension: the plan, and the evidence against the plan, both visible at once, so that anyone paying attention can see the argument and draw their own conclusion.

There is a small ethic in this, if you want one. Before you decide where people should walk, watch where they walk. Before you fill in the hedge, ask how long the hole has been there and who uses it. Before you rope off the grass, consider that the rope is a claim to know better than everyone who has crossed it, and that such claims are sometimes right and very often not. And when you find yourself on a path that no one built, take a second to notice it—the compressed earth, the roots exposed, the way it bends around a tree the planner never had to reckon with—because it is one of the few things in the built world that tells the truth without being asked.

The grass will grow back, eventually, if people stop. It always does. That's the other thing a desire line records: not just what people want, but that they're still wanting it, today, this morning, on their way in.
